title: Plain-language glossary for the Next-Generation HTML Atlas
note: Short, everyday definitions. Each term links to the atlas page where you can try it. Edit this file, then run python3 tools/atlas_build.py.

terms.definition: Designing so people with different bodies, senses and minds can all use something: by keyboard, screen reader, voice, magnification or simply on a tired day.
Software that plans and carries out several steps toward a goal. Safe agents ask a person before doing anything that changes data or costs money.
A short written description of an image, read aloud by screen readers and shown if the image cannot load. Decorative images get empty alt text so they are skipped.
A set of ready-made commands one program offers another. Browsers offer APIs for storage, sound, location and more, so pages do not have to build those from scratch.

terms.aka: accessible rich internet applications roles states
terms.definition: Extra HTML attributes that tell assistive technology what a custom control is and what state it is in. The first rule of ARIA: use a native HTML element instead whenever one exists.
A copy of your data saved as a file you control. Browser storage can be cleared, so exporting a backup is the only sure way to keep records long term.
The first measurement you compare later ones against, such as plant counts before restoration began. Without a baseline you cannot say what changed.
A browser feature that lets open tabs of the same site send each other messages instantly, without any server.
A stored copy of something fetched earlier, kept so it can be shown again quickly or without a connection.
An HTML element that scripts can paint on pixel by pixel. Used for charts, image editing and animation. Because it is just pixels, it needs a text alternative.
How much carbon dioxide is released to produce one unit of electricity where you are. It changes by country, season and hour, so energy estimates should let you set it.
A pattern that stops calling a failing service for a while after repeated errors, giving it time to recover instead of piling on more requests.
A clear, informed, freely given yes that can be withdrawn at any time. Real consent is specific, never assumed from silence and never bundled into something else.
A CSS rule that adapts a component to the space its container gives it, rather than to the whole screen, so the same card works in a sidebar and a main column.
A rule a page gives the browser listing where it may load or send things from. Every atlas page uses one to block connections to other websites.
How different two colours are in brightness, from 1:1 to 21:1. Body text needs at least 4.5:1 against its background to be readable for most people.
A plain text table format that any spreadsheet can open. Each line is a row and commas separate the columns.
Your own HTML tag, such as <seed-card>, defined once in JavaScript and reusable anywhere on a page with its behaviour built in.
Collecting only the data you truly need, for a stated purpose, and deleting it when that purpose ends. Data you never collect can never leak.
A box that appears over the page and asks for attention. The native <dialog> element handles keyboard focus and the Escape key for you.
A short fingerprint calculated from data. Change one character and the fingerprint changes completely, so it reveals tampering, but it cannot tell you whether the content is true.
Scrambling data so only someone with the right key can read it. It protects privacy when files are stored or shared.
Waiting longer after each failed attempt (for example 1, 2, then 4 seconds) before trying again, so a struggling connection is not flooded.
Checking whether the browser supports something before using it, then offering a simpler path if it does not.
The element that will respond to the keyboard right now, usually shown with an outline. Moving focus in a sensible order is essential for keyboard users.
A common text format for map features. Points are written longitude first, then latitude, which trips up many people.
The shortest distance between two points on a sphere, measured over the surface. It ignores roads and terrain, so it is not a travel route.
When an AI system states something fluent and confident that is not supported by any source. Citations and "I don't know" answers are the antidote.
A design where a person reviews and approves important steps an automated system proposes, instead of letting it act alone.
A database built into every modern browser. It holds much more than localStorage and works offline, but data stays on that one device.
The browser's built-in tool for writing dates, numbers, currencies and lists the way people expect in each language and region.
A simple text format for structured data, readable by people and by almost every programming language. Atlas backups are JSON files.
A way to describe a page's content (an article, an event, an organisation) in JSON so search engines and other tools can understand it.
A major area of a page, such as navigation or main content. Screen-reader users jump between landmarks the way sighted people glance around.
Part of a page that screen readers announce when its text changes, so a status like "Saved" is heard without moving focus.
Software that keeps your data on your own device first and works without a connection. Syncing or sharing is optional, never required.
A small, simple place in the browser to keep text between visits. Quick to use, limited in size, and can be cleared by the browser or the person.
A small file that tells the browser a site's name, icons and colours, so it can be installed like an app.
Information that describes content: its title, author, date, licence or language. Good metadata helps people and tools find and trust things.
Neighbours meeting each other's needs through voluntary, reciprocal help, rather than charity from above. Offers and needs are shared as equals.

terms.aka: compassionate communication observations feelings needs requests
terms.definition: A way of speaking that separates what happened from judgement, names feelings and needs, and makes requests the other person is free to decline.
Designing a tool to work fully without a connection, then using the network only as a bonus when it is there.
A way of describing colour by lightness, intensity and hue that matches human perception, which makes even, accessible colour scales easier to build.
The combination of scheme, host and port (like https://example.org). Browsers keep each origin's data and permissions separate for safety.
How much data a page makes a device download. Lighter pages load faster on weak connections and use less energy.
The browser's own question before a site can use sensitive things like location, camera or microphone. Good sites only ask after you choose an action that needs it.
Building a page that works in the simplest browser first, then adding richer features only where they are supported.
Where something came from and what happened to it since: who made it, when, from what sources, and who changed it.
A website that can be installed, opened from the home screen and used offline, built with ordinary web technology.
Answering questions by first finding relevant passages in trusted documents, then answering only from those passages with citations.
A device setting people use when animation causes dizziness, nausea or distraction. Respectful sites tone down or remove motion when it is on.
An agreed shape for data: which fields exist, what type each is, and which are required. Checking a schema stops broken files from corrupting your records.
Software that reads the screen aloud or to a braille display, used by many blind and low-vision people. It relies on good HTML structure.
A page delivered over an encrypted connection (or from your own computer). Many powerful browser features only work in secure contexts.
Using HTML elements for what they mean (a heading, a list, a button) rather than how they look, so browsers and assistive tools understand the page.
A small script a site installs in your browser that can save pages and serve them when you are offline.
A private inner structure for a web component, with its own styles that do not leak in or out.
Pictures described as shapes and text in code, so they stay sharp at any size and can be read and labelled for accessibility.
How far a measured value might be from the true value, written like 7.2 ± 0.3. Honest data always says how sure it is.
A browser feature that animates smoothly between two states of a page, or between pages, instead of jumping.
The international guidelines for accessible web content, organised as testable success criteria at levels A, AA and AAA.
A browser feature for generating, mixing and analysing sound in real time, entirely on your device.
A compact, fast format for running compiled code (from languages like Rust or C) safely inside the browser alongside JavaScript.
A script that runs in the background, separately from the page, so heavy work does not freeze buttons and scrolling.
Browser features that use a device's graphics hardware for fast drawing and computation. Always provide a simpler fallback.
A browser feature for virtual and augmented reality experiences on supported headsets and phones.
An attack where text someone typed is treated as code by a page. Showing untrusted text with textContent instead of innerHTML prevents it.
